<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

1: # Agentic ODI - AI Developer Guardrails
2: 
3: This file provides system instructions and guardrails for any AI agents (or LLMs) assisting with the development of the **Agentic ODI** project. Please adhere to these guidelines to maintain consistency and align with the project's vision.
4: 
5: > **Source of Truth for ODI Methodology**: `knowledge/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` by Anthony W. Ulwick (Strategyn). All ODI concepts in this project are grounded in that document. When in doubt, refer agents back to its definitions.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails
10: 
11: This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.
12: 
13: ### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?
14: 
15: ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.
16: 
17: ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done
22: 
23: - A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
24: - A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
25: - **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
26: - ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes
31: 
32: - **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
33: - Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
34: - **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):
35: 
36:   > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`
37: 
38:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
39:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
40:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
41:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.
42: 
43: - **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)
48: 
49: - All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
50:   1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
51:   2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
52:   3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
53:   4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
54:   5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
55:   6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
56:   7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
57:   8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs
58: 
59: - **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
60: - ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)
65: 
66: - Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
67:   - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
68:   - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?
69: 
70: - **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):
71: 
72:   ```
73:   Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
74:   ```
75: 
76: - **Interpretation**:
77:   - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
78:   - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
79:   - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.
80: 
81: - **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation
86: 
87: - ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
88: - Segments can be:
89:   - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
90:   - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
91:   - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value
92: 
93: - **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy
98: 
99: Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:
100: 
101: | Strategy | When to use |
102: |---|---|
103: | **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
104: | **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
105: | **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |
106: 
107: - **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent
112: 
113: These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:
114: 
115: | DO | DON'T |
116: |---|---|
117: | Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
118: | Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
119: | Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
120: | Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
121: | Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
122: | Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
123: | Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
128: - **Language**: Python 3.10+
129: - **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
130: - **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
131: - **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
132: - **UI / Chat Client**: `streamlit`
133: - **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
134: - **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
135: - **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail
140: 
141: `README.md` is the **primary human-facing source of truth** for this project. The agent MUST keep it current at all times.
142: 
143: ### When to update README.md
144: 
145: Update `README.md` whenever any of the following change:
146: 
147: | Change type | README section to update |
148: |---|---|
149: | New or removed Python file | **Code Overview** |
150: | New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | **Prerequisites** |
151: | New way to run the project | **Running the Environment** |
152: | New MCP tool or capability | **Code Overview** / relevant section |
153: | New workflow or agent instruction | **Getting Started → Agent-driven testing** |
154: | Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | **Deployment** |
155: | Roadmap item completed or added | **Roadmap & Next Steps** |
156: 
157: ### Rules
158: 
159: - ✅ **Update README in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
160: - ✅ **Keep the "Running the Environment" section accurate**: always reflect `python -m client.run` as the recommended launch command.
161: - ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
162: - ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
163: - ❌ **Never leave README in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.
164: 
165: ---
166: 
167: ## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails
168: 
169: ### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
170: - **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
171: - **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
172:   - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
173:   - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
174: - **Tool Creation**: 
175:   - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
176:   - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
177:   - **Capability Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update the `get_capabilities` tool's human-readable return string to ensure the capability set exactly matches the code.
178: 
179: ### 2. Async / Client Practices
180: - Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
181: - Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.
182: 
183: ### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
184: - Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
185: - When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.
186: 
187: ### 4. General Philosophy
188: - **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
189: - **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
190: - **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `connectors/` workspace package. New kinds implement `connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
191: - **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.
192: 
193: ### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
194: - **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
195: - **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
196: - **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `mcp_server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `connectors/src/connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
197: - **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
198: - **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
199: - **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
200: - **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

(End of file - total 200 lines)

## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails

This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.

### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?

ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.

ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.

---

### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done

- A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
- A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
- **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
- ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.

---

### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes

- **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
- Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
- **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):

  > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`

  - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
  - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
  - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
  - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.

- **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.

---

### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)

- All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
  1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
  2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
  3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
  4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
  5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
  6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
  7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
  8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs

- **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
- ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.

---

### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)

- Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
  - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
  - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?

- **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):

  ```
  Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
  ```

- **Interpretation**:
  - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
  - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
  - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.

- **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.

---

### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation

- ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
- Segments can be:
  - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
  - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
  - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value

- **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.

---

### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy

Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:

| Strategy | When to use |
|---|---|
| **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
| **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
| **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |

- **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.

---

### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent

These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:

| DO | DON'T |
|---|---|
| Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
| Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
| Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
| Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
| Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
| Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
| Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |

---

## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
- **Language**: Python 3.10+
- **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
- **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
- **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
- **UI / Chat Client**: `streamlit`
- **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
- **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
- **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`

---

## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail

`README.md` is the **primary human-facing source of truth** for this project. The agent MUST keep it current at all times.

### When to update README.md

Update `README.md` whenever any of the following change:

| Change type | README section to update |
|---|---|
| New or removed Python file | **Code Overview** |
| New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | **Prerequisites** |
| New way to run the project | **Running the Environment** |
| New MCP tool or capability | **Code Overview** / relevant section |
| New workflow or agent instruction | **Getting Started → Agent-driven testing** |
| Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | **Deployment** |
| Roadmap item completed or added | **Roadmap & Next Steps** |

### Rules

- ✅ **Update README in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
- ✅ **Keep the "Running the Environment" section accurate**: always reflect `python -m client.run` as the recommended launch command.
- ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
- ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
- ❌ **Never leave README in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.

---

## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails

### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
- **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
- **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
  - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
  - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
- **Tool Creation**: 
  - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
  - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
  - **Capability Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update the `get_capabilities` tool's human-readable return string to ensure the capability set exactly matches the code.

### 2. Async / Client Practices
- Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
- Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.

### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
- Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
- When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.

### 4. General Philosophy
- **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
- **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
- **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `connectors/` workspace package. New kinds implement `connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
- **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.

### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
- **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
- **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
- **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `mcp_server/src/mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `mcp_server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `connectors/src/connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
- **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
- **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
- **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
- **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

An installed Living Studio could never update itself. The Tauri app was pinned at `0.1.0` while releases are cut at `0.11.0`, `Tauri Release` had never run (release-please publishes through the API, which never emits a `push: tags` event), no release carried a `latest.json`, and the only update affordance was a button buried in Settings that installed without asking and never relaunched.

This makes self-update real end to end.

## What a person experiences

- Four seconds after launch — never competing with first paint — the app checks quietly. It re-checks every six hours and when the window returns to the foreground after that long.
- A found update downloads in the background. One bar above the conversation shows progress; it never blocks, never takes focus, and can be dismissed.
- macOS and Linux stage the update as soon as its signature verifies, so it applies on the next ordinary launch even if nobody clicks anything. **Restart now** applies it immediately. Windows needs the app to exit for NSIS, so it offers **Update & restart**.
- **Settings → Software update** shows the running version, a plain-language status, the release notes, **Check now**, **Skip this version**, and the auto-check toggle. Check failures stay here instead of interrupting the conversation.
- The top bar shows the running version and quietly becomes **Update ready** when a restart will finish the job; both open the update settings.
- In the browser and in `tauri dev`, the section says honestly that in-app updates live in the installed desktop app.

## Architecture

```
apps/studio/src/updater/
  types.ts        domain vocabulary
  machine.ts      pure reducer + selectors (no I/O, no timers, no React)
  service.ts      schedule → check → download → install → relaunch, injected transport/storage/clock
  transport.ts    the only module that imports Tauri plugins
  platform.ts     macOS/Linux stage silently; Windows binds install to the explicit restart
  UpdateProvider.tsx  one service per app, shared via useSyncExternalStore
  UpdateBanner.tsx    the quiet bar
  UpdateSettings.tsx  the Settings section
```

Every surface derives from one snapshot, so the bar, the sidebar, and Settings cannot disagree. Background-check failures are silent by selector, not by convention.

`tauri-plugin-process` is registered with `process:default` for the in-place relaunch. The branch is rebased onto the one-room shell (`StudioBar`), so the indicator lives in the top bar.

## Release pipeline

- `release-please` now bumps `apps/studio/package.json`, `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, and `apps/studio/src-tauri/Cargo.toml` from `extra-files`; without this the installed version can never move.
- `Tauri Release` and `release` also trigger on `release: published`, which is the event release-please actually produces. `push: tags` stays for hand-cut tags.
- A new `verify` job fails the release if `latest.json` does not advertise the tag's version and carry signed artifacts for Linux, Windows, and both macOS architectures.
- The desktop version is synced to the current `0.12.0` so local builds match the manifest.

## Verification

- `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test -- --run` (**267 tests**), `npm run build`.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, `cargo check`.
- **Real end-to-end proof**, not a mock: `scripts/verify-desktop-update.sh` builds two signed AppImages with a throwaway key, serves a local `latest.json`, runs 0.1.0, and watches it replace its own file:

```
OK: the running 0.1.0 replaced its own AppImage with 0.2.0
OK: the updated app reports no update and downloads nothing
```

  The installed file's sha256 equals the 0.2.0 build's, and the second run hit `/latest.json` without requesting the bundle — so the updater checked, downloaded, verified the signature, installed, and then correctly reported itself current.

## Notes

- The relaunch itself is covered by unit tests and is the canonical `@tauri-apps/plugin-process` `relaunch()` call; the E2E cannot click a button in a headless environment.
- Linux self-update applies to AppImage installs. A `.deb` install surfaces a clear error instead of silently doing nothing.
- This PR does not publish a release. The first release built after merge should be the first one that ships a working `latest.json`; the new `verify` job makes a failure loud.
- Design and plan: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-21-studio-auto-update-design.md`, `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-21-studio-auto-update.md`.

# Agentic ODI [![CI](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![uv](https://img.shields.io/badge/uv-managed-green)](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) [![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) [![FastMCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastMCP-powered-orange)](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) [![pytest](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-pytest-blue)](https://pytest.org) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/Model%20Context%20Protocol-enabled-8A2BE2)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) > **Experimental test to learn and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) specifications.**
--- ## 📋 Table of Contents - [The Vision: Context-Aware Innovation](#-the-vision-context-aware-innovation) - [Current State (Experimental Testbed)](#-current-state-experimental-testbed) - [Code Overview](#-code-overview) - [Getting Started](#-getting-started) - [Command-Line Interface (CLI)](#-command-line-interface-cli) - [Interactive Chat](#-interactive-chat) - [Manage Customer Outcomes](#-manage-customer-outcomes) - [External Connectors (MCP Ingest)](#-external-connectors-mcp-ingest) - [Living Studio Run Modes](#-living-studio-run-modes) - [Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend](#-local-tools-capable-llm-backend-for-mcp-testing) - [Agent-Driven Testing](#-agent-driven-testing) - [Linting, Formatting & Type Checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) - [Testing](#-testing) - [Test Coverage](#-test-coverage) - [Test Coverage Map](#-test-coverage-map) - [Agent Session Tracking](#-agent-session-tracking) - [Superpowers with Pi](#-superpowers-with-pi) - [Developer Workflow for Formatting](#-developer-workflow-for-formatting) - [Superpowers with Freebuff](#-superpowers-with-freebuff) - [Quick Install (Binary)](#quick-install-binary) - [Release automation](#release-automation) - [Deployment](#-deployment) - [Roadmap & Next Steps](#-roadmap--next-steps) - [Contributing](#-contributing) - [License](#-license) --- ## 🌟 The Vision: Context-Aware Innovation ## 🎯 Intent-First Experience for Product Managers The Living Studio has been redesigned to focus on **product managers' ambition** rather than ODI methodology. The agent now interprets PMs' career-defining opportunities and helps them win them, rather than explaining frameworks. **North Star:** Help me choose and win the next opportunity that matters — to customers, the business, and my career. **Key Features:** 1. **Intent-First Agent**: The system prompt has been rewritten to prioritize PM ambition and silent translation of ODI concepts into actionable outcomes. The agent now proposes observations and asks for confirmation, creating a "living memory" of the conversation. 2. **Local Studio Memory**: A SQLite-backed store persists conversations and observations (`career`, `opportunity`, `business`, etc.) across sessions. The "What I've learned" panel shows these observations and allows the PM to confirm, edit, or dismiss them. 3. **Opportunity Thesis**: The default canvas focus is the **Opportunity Thesis** card, which presents one opportunity with its importance, current state, and the gap to be closed. This replaces the traditional Opportunity Landscape. 4. **Ambition-Driven Onboarding**: The first-run wizard now presents four doors based on the PM's intent: - "I have an opportunity in mind" - "My boss handed me a priority" - "I need to find one" - "Pressure-test an idea" 5. **Session Persistence**: Conversations are persisted via the `conversationId` and `memory` SSE events, allowing the PM to resume from where they left off. 6. **Explainability**: The agent uses a `remember` tool to propose observations, which are stored in the local memory store and displayed in the MemoryPanel. The implementation leverages the same underlying ODI engine but with a new UI and interaction model focused on PM outcomes. --- ## 🏗️ Current State (Experimental Testbed) This repository serves as an initial sandbox for understanding server-client MCP communication streams. We are utilizing [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) to prototype HTTP-based context delivery. --- ## 🧩 Code Overview This repository is a [uv workspace](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/workspaces/) made up of **six** installable Python projects plus the React `studio/` front end, each with its own build, tests, and layout: | Package | Description | |---|---| | **`core/`** (`agentic-odi-core`) | Domain models, the `ODIService` business-logic layer, and repository implementations (in-memory and SQLite), including ODI opportunity-score computation. | | **`mcp_server/`** (`agentic-odi-mcp-server`) | A foundational MCP Server exposing an HTTP transport layer. It hosts tools for Jobs, Steps, Desired Outcomes, and Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value). | | **`local_server/`** (`agentic-odi-local-server`) | The FastAPI **Living Studio sidecar**. It talks to the MCP server on the client's behalf and serves the Studio API — configuration, health probes, canvas data, MCP mutations, and streaming (SSE) chat with the LLM tool-loop — plus the built SPA when `studio/dist` exists. | | **`client/`** (`agentic-odi-client`) | The local dev **launcher** (`run.py` / `python -m client.run`) that starts the MCP server and the Studio sidecar together. (Its former Streamlit UI has been replaced by the `studio/` SPA.) | | **`studio/`** (React + TypeScript + Vite) | **The Living Studio** front end — a spatial, conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation with an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous copilot. Ships as a browser SPA and as a **Tauri 2 desktop app** (`studio/src-tauri/`). | | **`cli/`** (`agentic-odi-cli`) | A [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based command-line interface with an interactive chat mode plus `version`, `update`, `connectors`, and `customer-outcomes` (alias `outcomes`) commands. Data commands are local-first (`--backend local`, default) or remote (`--backend mcp`), with readable tables, `--json`, and a top-level `score`. | | **`connectors/`** (`agentic-odi-connectors`) | Pluggable external integrations. The first kind is an **MCP client connector** that connects to a remote MCP server over HTTP, checks health, and ingests tools/resources into a local ingest sink. Additional kinds (REST, webhooks, and so on) can register against the same protocol later. | --- ## 🚀 Getting Started ### Prerequisites - **Python** 3.10+ - [**uv**](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager Install the entire workspace (all six projects plus dev tooling): ```bash uv sync --all-packages ``` This creates a `.venv` and installs `agentic-odi-core`, `agentic-odi-mcp-server`, `agentic-odi-local-server`, `agentic-odi-client`, `agentic-odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi-connectors` in editable mode. ### 💻 Command-Line Interface (CLI) The [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based CLI lets you interact with Agentic ODI directly from your terminal. It provides an interactive chat mode plus version, update, and data commands. Data commands are **local-first**: they read and write a SQLite store with no server required, and switch to a remote MCP server with `--backend mcp`. Launch it with: ```bash python -m cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version python -m cli --help # show available options and commands python -m cli # start interactive chat in a terminal (help when piped) ``` A console script is also installed, so `agentic-odi --version` works the same way. **Global options:** | Option | Environment variable | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `--backend local\|mcp` | `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` | `local` | Run in-process against SQLite, or call a remote MCP server. | | `--db PATH` | `AGENTIC_ODI_DB` | `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db` | Store path for the `local` backend. | | `--mcp-url URL` | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | Server URL for the `mcp` backend. | Data commands print readable tables and blocks by default; add `--json` for machine-readable output. Diagnostics go to stderr and failures exit non-zero (`0` success, `1` error, `2` usage error). ### 💬 Interactive Chat `agentic-odi chat` (or simply `agentic-odi` in a terminal) starts a conversational session against the MCP server and an OpenAI-compatible LLM. Responses stream to the terminal, and the assistant can call the ODI MCP tools as it talks. ```bash agentic-odi chat agentic-odi chat --model local-tools-model --mcp-url http://localhost:8000/mcp ``` Before starting, run the MCP server (`python -m mcp_server`) and point the chat at an OpenAI-compatible model endpoint. The chat reads the same environment variables as the Living Studio: | Variable | Default | CLI flag | |---|---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | `--base-url` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | `--model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | `--api-key` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | `--mcp-url` | Inside the session, `/help` lists the commands, `/tools` lists the MCP tools the assistant can call, `/clear` resets the conversation, and `/exit` (or `/quit`) ends the session. > [!NOTE] > Chat is the only CLI mode that needs an LLM endpoint. The `customer-outcomes` and `connectors` commands keep working without one. ### 🎯 Manage Customer Outcomes Customer Outcomes link customer value to business value. The `local` backend writes to the shared SQLite store with no server required; add `--backend mcp` to route through a running MCP server (`python -m mcp_server`). The group is also available under its historical name `outcomes`. ```bash # Add a Customer Outcome agentic-odi customer-outcomes add --job-id --direction minimize --unit "time" --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn" # List outcomes (optionally filtered, or as JSON) agentic-odi customer-outcomes list agentic-odi customer-outcomes list --job-id agentic-odi customer-outcomes list --json # Get, update, delete agentic-odi customer-outcomes get agentic-odi customer-outcomes update --importance 9.0 agentic-odi customer-outcomes delete --yes # Compute ODI Opportunity Score (top-level, also under the group) agentic-odi score 8 2 agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2 ``` Set `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` (or `--mcp-url`) to point to a non-default server when using `--backend mcp`. ### 🔌 External Connectors (MCP Ingest) Connectors are named integrations stored in `.agentic-odi/connectors.json` (or a path you pass with `--config` / `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`). The first kind is `mcp`: Agentic ODI acts as an MCP **client** and pulls catalog, resources, and optional tool results from an external MCP **server**. The fastest way to connect is a preset. `connectors catalog` lists every built-in preset, grouped by the capability area it serves: ```bash python -m cli connectors catalog # all presets python -m cli connectors catalog --area strategy-alignment python -m cli connectors catalog --json ``` | Capability area (`--area`) | Presets | |---|---| | Voice of customer & qualitative research (`voice-of-customer`) | `notion`, `gong`, `fireflies`, `intercom`, `confluence` | | Quantitative data & opportunity scoring (`quantitative-data`) | `posthog`, `amplitude`, `mixpanel` | | Market & competitive intelligence (`market-intelligence`) | `exa`, `tavily` | | Product strategy & backlog alignment (`strategy-alignment`) | `linear`, `github`, `jira`, `miro`, `figma` | | Strategy & knowledge management output (`knowledge-output`) | `slack` | Register one with `--preset`; `--name` defaults to the preset id: ```bash # Token-based preset: export the variable it needs first export GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=ghp_... python -m cli connectors add mcp --preset github python -m cli connectors health --name github python -m cli connectors ingest --name github # OAuth-based preset: the browser consent flow starts on first use python -m cli connectors add mcp --preset notion ``` Credentials never enter the registry. Presets that use API keys store `${VAR}` placeholders that are resolved from the environment when a connection is opened, and `connectors health` names any variable that is missing. `--url` overrides the endpoint (self-hosted or proxied deployments) and `--tool` still selects which tools to call during ingest. Custom servers keep working the same way: ```bash python -m cli connectors add mcp --name internal --url https://mcp.internal.example/mcp --tool latest_quote python -m cli connectors list ``` Ingested records are normalized (`catalog`, `resource`, `tool_result`) and appended to the in-process ingest sink. They are not written into the ODI jobs/outcomes store. > [!NOTE] > Presets cover MCP servers with a hosted endpoint. Servers you run yourself (Snowflake, BigQuery, Google Drive, Brave Search, and similar) are added with an explicit `--url`. The catalog lives in `connectors/src/connectors/catalog.py`. > [!NOTE] > OAuth tokens are cached in memory for the life of one CLI process, so an OAuth preset may ask for consent again on the next `connectors health` or `connectors ingest`. Prefer a token-based preset where the server offers one. ### ⚡ Living Studio Run Modes The Living Studio runs three ways. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM directly. **Architecture** ```text ┌────────────────────────────┐ /api (JSON) ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Living Studio SPA │ ────────────▶ │ local_server (sidecar) │ │ React + TS + Vite │ /api/chat │ FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100 │ │ (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │ - config / health / canvas │ └────────────────────────────┘ SSE stream │ - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │ │ - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop) │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ │ MCP (HTTP) ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ mcp_server :8000/mcp │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ▲ │ OpenAI-compatible ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐ │ Your local LLM backend │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ``` **1. Web — production build (recommended for a quick look)** ```bash npm --prefix studio run build # build the SPA into studio/dist python -m client.run # starts MCP :8000 + sidecar :8100 ``` | Service | URL | |---|---| | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | | Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 | **2. Web — dev with hot reload** (Vite proxies `/api` to the sidecar): ```bash npm --prefix studio run dev:full # MCP + sidecar + Vite together # open http://localhost:5173 ``` **3. Desktop — Tauri 2** (the app spawns the MCP server and sidecar itself): ```bash npm --prefix studio run tauri dev # dev window npm --prefix studio run tauri build # bundles: .deb / .AppImage (Linux), .app / .dmg (macOS), .msi / .exe (Windows) ``` > [!NOTE] > **Tauri prerequisites.** The desktop build needs the WebKitGTK toolchain and Rust 1.90+. On Debian/Ubuntu: > > ```bash > sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential pkg-config curl wget file \ > libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf xdg-utils libfuse2t64 > ``` > > The Tauri CLI ships as the `@tauri-apps/cli` npm dev dependency (`npm --prefix studio run tauri`). The sidecar is launched with `uv run python -m …` from the repository root; if the app cannot locate the repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`. #### 🔐 Desktop signing & updater secrets Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub Actions secrets. | Secret | Purpose | |---|---| | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate`. | | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). | | `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. | | `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. | | `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. | | `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. | Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via **Settings → Check for updates**. #### 🔑 Managing the updater signing key The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is embedded in `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in CI, or attached to a build artifact. 1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it: ```bash npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f ``` This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub` (public). 2. **Paste the public key** into `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`: ```jsonc { "plugins": { "updater": { "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"], "pubkey": "" } } } ``` 3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions: ```bash mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/ chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key ``` Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives. Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing installs. 4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI: ```bash gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body "" # only if you set a password ``` 5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed): ```bash gh secret list ``` 6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public key ahead of the cut-over. > [!CAUTION] > If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI (`client/src/client/app.py`) has been removed. The Living Studio now lives in `studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop app) and is served by the `local_server` sidecar on port **8100** (previously Streamlit's `8501`). Start everything with `python -m client.run`. All `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI formulas are unchanged. ### 🧠 Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend (for MCP testing) To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a local LLM backend that: - Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example, `/v1/chat/completions`), and - Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**. A simple fully local option is [`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server. 1. **Install a local LLM server** Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for platform-specific build notes): ```bash pip install llama-cpp-python ``` 2. **Download a small tools-capable model** Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a 7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g. `C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`. 3. **Start the OpenAI-compatible server** Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default used by the Living Studio sidecar: ```bash python -m llama_cpp.server \ --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \ --model_alias local-tools-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \ --chat_format openai ``` This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`. 4. **Point the Living Studio at the local server** The sidecar reads defaults from environment variables (with sensible fallbacks): | Variable | Default | |---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Living Studio's **Settings** panel. 5. **Verify tool-calling against the MCP server** - (Optional) Before starting the UI, confirm the LLM backend is reachable: ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1/models ``` If this request fails, fix your local LLM server configuration before debugging the MCP client/server. - Start the MCP server and the Living Studio (via `python -m client.run` or `npm --prefix studio run dev:full`). - In the browser UI, ask the assistant something that should use ODI tools, for example: “Help me define a new Job-to-be-Done and add it to your ODI repository.” - You should see the assistant briefly display that it is calling tools (for example, `add_job`, `get_jobs`, etc.) and then respond with grounded ODI guidance, confirming that the local LLM, MCP server, and client wiring all work together. - If the LLM backend is unreachable or misconfigured, the UI will show a clear error banner indicating that the backend at your configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps above to fix your local LLM setup. ### 🤖 Agent-Driven Testing Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it will start both processes, open the browser, send a test message, and report the results. --- ## 🧹 Linting, Formatting & Type Checks (CI parity) The CI pipeline runs several quality checks. You can mirror them locally with: ```bash # Ruff lint and formatting checks (per-file config comes from each project's pyproject.toml) uv run ruff check . uv run ruff format --check . # Type checking (run per project so each project's config applies) uv run --directory core mypy . uv run --directory mcp_server mypy . uv run --directory local_server mypy . uv run --directory client mypy . uv run --directory cli mypy . uv run --directory connectors mypy . # Security scanning uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src local_server/src cli/src client/src connectors/src # Tests (same as CI) uv run --directory core pytest uv run --directory mcp_server pytest uv run --directory local_server pytest uv run --directory client pytest uv run --directory cli pytest uv run --directory connectors pytest ``` ### 🖥️ Frontend & Desktop Checks (studio) The SPA and Tauri shell mirror their CI jobs locally: ```bash npm --prefix studio run lint # ESLint npm --prefix studio run typecheck # tsc --noEmit npm --prefix studio test -- --run # Vitest (run once) npm --prefix studio run build # production build → studio/dist cd studio/src-tauri && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check ``` To run these automatically before each commit, enable the bundled pre-commit hooks: ```bash uv tool install pre-commit pre-commit install ``` After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` will run on staged files whenever you commit. You can also trigger them manually with: ```bash pre-commit run --all-files ``` --- ## ✅ Testing Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely in-memory — no running server required. Each project owns its tests: ```bash uv run --directory core pytest uv run --directory mcp_server pytest uv run --directory local_server pytest uv run --directory client pytest uv run --directory cli pytest uv run --directory connectors pytest ``` ### 📈 Test Coverage CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12**, combines each package's coverage into one `coverage.xml`, and uploads it to [Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi) from the 3.12 job. Each matrix job also stores its combined report as a build artifact. The Codecov upload authenticates with the `CODECOV_TOKEN` repository secret and is non-blocking (`fail_ci_if_error: false`), so a Codecov outage or a fork PR without secrets cannot fail the test job. The badge at the top of this README tracks `main`, which is the baseline every PR is compared against: - **Project** status requires at least **90%** coverage (`target: 90%`) and tolerates a 1% dip from `codecov.yml`. - **Patch** status is informational for now, so new code can land while the suite catches up. To reproduce the combined report locally, run each package with its own coverage file and merge them the way CI does: ```bash set -e for pkg in core mcp_server local_server client cli connectors; do # Absolute path, so each package writes to the repo root rather than its own directory. COVERAGE_FILE="$PWD/.coverage.$pkg" uv run --directory "$pkg" pytest --cov="$pkg" -q done uv run coverage combine .coverage.* uv run coverage xml -o coverage.xml && uv run coverage report ``` > [!NOTE] > Coverage is only collected for the Python packages. `studio/` and test directories are excluded in `codecov.yml`. ### 📊 Test Coverage Map | File | What it covers | |---|---| | `core/tests/test_models.py` | Domain models and ODI opportunity-score computation | | `core/tests/test_service.py` | `ODIService` jobs/steps/outcomes and Customer Outcome CRUD | | `core/tests/test_sqlite_repository.py` | SQLite event-sourced repository: snapshot reload, updates, deletes, and clear | | `core/tests/test_intent_store.py` | Append-only Intent Store reads, clear, and legacy blank payloads | | `core/tests/test_repository.py` | In-memory repository filtering and update/delete edge cases | | `core/tests/test_messages.py` | Shared framework guidelines and not-found helpers | | `mcp_server/tests/test_odi.py` | Full ODI workflow (add job → steps → outcomes → retrieval) + capabilities tool | | `mcp_server/tests/test_customer_outcomes.py` | Customer - Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named `test_*.py`. - Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`. - Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests. - The server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before each test. > [!TIP] > Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the results automatically. ### 🧪 Agent Session Tracking Agent sessions are captured with the [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/overview) CLI. The repository integration lives in `.entire/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, and `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. Run `entire status` to confirm it is enabled and `entire checkpoint list` to inspect captured checkpoints. --- ## 🤝 Superpowers with Pi This project includes [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) as a [Pi package](https://pi.dev/docs/packages). When using [Pi](https://pi.dev) with this project, Superpowers skills and extensions are automatically loaded. To enable: 1. Install Pi: `curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh` 2. Trust the project (first time only): `pi config --local --approve` 3. Start Pi: `pi` The `.pi/settings.json` declares the Superpowers package. Pi will clone it and load: - **Extension**: `superpowers.ts` — injects the `using-superpowers` bootstrap at session startup and after compaction - **Skills**: 12 Superpowers skills (TDD, subagent-driven-development, systematic-debugging, etc.) > [!NOTE] > Superpowers is also available for OpenCode via the plugin in `opencode.json`. The Pi package provides native Pi integration without needing the OpenCode compatibility layer. ### 🧼 Developer Workflow for Formatting - **When editing Python files**, either: - Rely on the **pre-commit hooks** above (recommended), or - Run Ruff formatting directly before pushing: ```bash uv run ruff format . ``` - **CI behavior**: - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files. - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only. - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the changes, and push again. ## 🤖 Superpowers with Freebuff This project ships [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) for [Freebuff](https://freebuff.com) as repo-local skills plus a session-start bootstrap. No plugin or hook is required: - **Skills**: `.agents/skills/` contains 15 Superpowers skills. Freebuff discovers them automatically; load one with the `skill` tool. - **Bootstrap**: `AGENTS.md` injects the `using-superpowers` rules and the Freebuff tool mapping at session start. - **Mapping**: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/freebuff-tools.md` maps skill actions to Freebuff tools. Start Freebuff in the repository and ask "What are your superpowers?" to verify. See [docs/superpowers/freebuff-setup.md](docs/superpowers/freebuff-setup.md) for update and troubleshooting notes. --- ## Quick Install (Binary) Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Install the latest release with one command: ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` The installer places the binary under `~/.local/share/agentic-odi/versions//`, creates a `current` symlink, and symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`. If `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH, add it (e.g., `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`). On Windows, the PowerShell installer uses `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\` and copies `.exe` files to `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\bin\`. ### Update By default, `odi` auto-checks for updates once every 24 hours and applies the update on the next run (auto-update is enabled by default). Control behavior with: - `odi update` — explicit check and update - `--no-update` flag — skip auto-update for this run - `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1` — disable auto-update globally When running from a non-frozen source install, auto-update is suppressed automatically. ### Install layout ``` ~/.local/share/agentic-odi/ ├── versions// │ └── odi (and bundled files) └── current -> versions/ ~/.local/bin/ ├── odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi ├── odipm ├── odi-cli └── agentic-odi ~/.config/agentic-odi/ # state/preferences ``` Environment variables: `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` (override install root), `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_BIN_HOME`. The default backend is `local` (`--backend local`); no MCP server is required. ### Unsigned binaries macOS may quarantine downloaded binaries: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/odi` (if needed). Windows SmartScreen may show a warning for unsigned binaries; choose "More info → Run anyway" if you trust the release. ### Release automation Releases are cut and published by CI with no approval step: 1. Conventional commits land on `main`; `release-please` opens or updates the release PR. 2. The `release-please` workflow arms auto-merge on that PR. `main` requires the `CI green` check (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), so the PR merges itself as soon as CI passes — nobody clicks merge. 3. The merge cuts tag `vX.Y.Z` and the GitHub Release; the tag starts the `release` and `Tauri Release` workflows, which attach the CLI archives, `checksums.txt`, the install scripts, and the desktop bundles to it. 4. `e2e-install` runs after `release` succeeds and installs the published binary on Linux, macOS, and Windows. **One-time setup (GitHub App).** GitHub holds workflow runs that start from `GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored pushes ("This workflow requires approval from a maintainer") and ignores the tag such a push creates, which is why releases used to need a maintainer. A release-only GitHub App avoids both: 1. Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App, with permissions: Contents `Read and write`, Issues `Read and write`, Pull requests `Read and write` (no webhook). 2. Install the App on this repository. 3. Add repository secrets `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the App's client ID) and `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (a generated private key). Until those secrets exist, the `release-please` workflow logs a warning and falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`: releases still happen, but the release PR needs a maintainer approval and merge, and the tag will not start the asset builds. After adding the secrets, re-run the workflow (`gh workflow run release-please.yml`) or push to `main` so the open release PR is re-driven by the App. To check the installer without cutting a release, run `bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh` — it serves a simulated release over HTTP and exercises `scripts/install.sh` end to end (CI runs it too). ## ☁️ Deployment The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**, Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents. ### 🧪 Test Chat (UI) Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)** ### 🔌 MCP Server Endpoint Integrate via the MCP protocol at: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)** > [!IMPORTANT] > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a client. --- ## 🗺️ Roadmap & Next Steps As we validate the feasibility of this architecture, our next milestones include: - [x] **External MCP client connector**: Pluggable connectors package with an HTTP MCP ingest client, CLI adapter, and in-memory tests. - [ ] **Map ingested evidence onto ODI artifacts**: Turn connector records into jobs, outcomes, or evidence without mixing connector plumbing into the ODI store. - [ ] **Additional connector kinds**: REST/webhooks and similar integrations implementing the same `Connector` protocol. - [ ] **ODI Schema Definition**: Define standardized Pydantic models for *Jobs*, *Steps*, and *Outcomes*. - [x] **CLI Dataset Commands**: Extend `cli/` so the ODI dataset can be created, queried, and scored from the terminal, in addition to the current MCP path. - [ ] **Context Tooling**: Replace the dummy `greet` tool with capabilities like `get_job_map(job_id)` or `evaluate_outcome(statement)`. - [ ] **Data Persistence Layer**: Connect the fastmcp server to a lightweight vector or relational database containing actual user research data. - [ ] **Agentic Integration**: Hook the client up to an LLM (e.g., via LangChain or standard OpenAI clients) so the LLM can *discover* the ODI tools and intelligently request customer insights when ideating features. --- ## 🤝 Contributing Contributions are welcome! This project uses [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for linting and formatting and [pytest](https://pytest.org/) for tests. Please ensure any change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) before opening a pull request. --- ## 📄 License No license has been specified for this repository yet. Until one is added, all rights reserved by the maintainers. Please reach out before reuse or redistribution. ---
